context: process EPC · reformer, compressors and high-pressure loops; system-by-system commissioning

brief.intro: New to this project type? A nitrogen fertilizer complex turns natural gas, air and water into ammonia, and ammonia and carbon dioxide into urea granules. The ammonia plant reforms gas into hydrogen in a large fired furnace (the reformer), cleans it, and reacts it with nitrogen at high pressure and temperature in the synthesis loop, driven by very large compressors. The urea plant reacts ammonia with CO2 at high pressure in special corrosion-resistant equipment, concentrates the solution and forms it into granules or prills, which go to a large storage shed and ship loaders. Around these sit utilities as big as a power plant — steam, cooling water, demineralised water — plus ammonia storage tanks. It is a classic process-plant job: heavy foundations, tall structures, kilometres of piping in exotic materials, and a long commissioning that brings systems into service in a fixed order.

scope.desc: Flushing, blowing, catalyst loading, reformer dry-out, first ammonia, first urea and the performance test.

must_get_right: Compressors, the reformer, high-pressure urea equipment and the synthesis converter are ordered first; their vendor data also releases the foundation design.
Piping is the bulk of the man-hours: prefabrication rate, erection, stress-relief, NDT and hydrotest must be planned by system and tracked by weld count.
Utilities must be running months before the process units — steam, cooling water, air and power are needed to commission everything else.
Switch from area-based construction to system-based completion early; the start-up order (utilities → reformer → ammonia → urea) fixes which systems must be finished first.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Construction is organised by unit and area; from mechanical completion onward the schedule is organised by system and test pack, in the start-up order.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Site calendar with extended shifts in peak piping months; commissioning and start-up run around the clock.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Engineering and vendor data → piling and foundations → structures and equipment → piping → electrical, instruments, insulation → mechanical completion by system → pre-commissioning. Start-up order: utilities → reformer and front end → synthesis loop (first ammonia) → urea plant (first urea) → performance test. The critical path runs through the compressors or the HP equipment, then the piping of the last system in the start-up order.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Licensor packages and vendor data arrive on the agreed dates; natural gas, power and water are available for commissioning; heavy-lift cranes and transport routes are secured for the delivery windows.

sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Congested plot with simultaneous heavy lifts and piping; hot work near live gas after the first systems are commissioned; specialist welders for alloy and stainless materials.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late vendor data, long-lead equipment delivery, piping productivity and weld repair rate, compressor commissioning problems, and catalyst or leak issues at start-up. Contingency is held before mechanical completion and before first ammonia.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by unit / area, then system; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the piping, mechanical and commissioning teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
